A_paper.answer: The hierarchical modelling approach assumes that each group-specific embedding vector is drawn from a distribution centered on a fixed hyperparameter, tying the per-group vectors together through a common prior distribution [1]. This hierarchical structure allows sharing statistical strength among the per-group variables, and the regularization term then applies only to the global vectors and the hyperparameter rather than the per-group vectors [1]. The model is fit by maximizing the resulting objective with respect to the per-group embeddings, global vectors, and hyperparameter using stochastic gradient ascent [1]. This hierarchical embedding structure is one of two proposed methods—the other being amortization—for tying individual group-specific embeddings together to share statistical strength, both of which introduce a set of global embedding vectors from which the group-specific vectors are generated [4].

A_paper.answer: The refine decoder masks each word in the summary draft one by one, then feeds the draft to BERT to generate context vectors, and predicts the n-th refined word given the other words of the summary [5]. This process is similar to the cloze task in BERT's pre-train process, so by using the ability of the contextual language model the decoder can generate more fluent and natural sequences [1]. A_paper.question: How is the vocabulary of word-like or phoneme-like units automatically discovered?
A_paper.answer: The vocabulary of word-like units is discovered via unsupervised term discovery (UTD), which thresholds graph edges so that each connected component of the graph is a cluster of acoustic segments producing a corresponding term (word/phrase) category, with each cluster consisting of a list of term occurrences [3]. The weight on each graph edge can be exact DTW-based similarity or other heuristic similarity, and a separate logistic regression model can rescore the similarity between identified matches by determining how likely the matching pair is the same underlying word/phrase and is not a filled pause [3]. UTD aims to identify and cluster repeating word-like units across speech based around segmental dynamic time warping (DTW) [5]. Alternatively, phoneme-like units are discovered through a model-based approach, i.e., unsupervised learning of hidden Markov model (HMM) based phoneme-like units from untranscribed speech [5]. Specifically, a phone-loop model is formulated where each phoneme-like unit is modeled as an HMM with a Gaussian mixture model of output densities (GMM-HMM), and under the Dirichlet process framework the phone loop is considered as an infinite mixture of GMM-HMMs with mixture weights based on the stick-breaking construction of the Dirichlet process [1]. The infinite number of units in the mixture is truncated in practice, giving zero mixture weight to any unit beyond some large count, and this mixture of GMM-HMMs is treated as a single unified HMM so that segmentation of the data is performed using the standard forward-backward algorithm [1]. Training is fully unsupervised and parallelized, and after a fixed number of training iterations the Viterbi decoding algorithm is used to obtain acoustic unit tokenizations of the data [1].

B_paper_rr24.question: How is the vocabulary of word-like or phoneme-like units automatically discovered?
B_paper_rr24.answer: The vocabulary of word-like units is automatically discovered through unsupervised term discovery (UTD), which identifies and clusters repeated terms such as words or phrases from speech [1]. To circumvent the exhaustive DTW-based search limited by time complexity, the scalable UTD framework in the Zero Resource Toolkit (ZRTools) is exploited, permitting search in reduced time [1][3]. The UTD procedures in ZRTools involve constructing sparse approximate acoustic similarity matrices between pairs of speech utterances, identifying word repetitions via fast diagonal line search and segmental DTW, constructing an acoustic similarity graph where nodes represent matching acoustic segments and edges reflect DTW distances, and thresholding the graph edges so that each connected component is a cluster of acoustic segments producing a corresponding term category [3]. The vocabulary of phoneme-like units is automatically discovered through acoustic unit discovery (AUD), an unsupervised model-based approach that learns hidden Markov model (HMM) based phoneme-like units from untranscribed speech [1]. Specifically, a phone-loop model is formulated where each phoneme-like unit is modeled as an HMM with a Gaussian mixture model of output densities (GMM-HMM), and under the Dirichlet process framework the phone loop is considered an infinite mixture of GMM-HMMs with mixture weights based on the stick-breaking construction of the Dirichlet process [2][3]. Training is fully unsupervised and parallelized, and after a fixed number of training iterations the Viterbi decoding algorithm is used to obtain acoustic unit tokenizations of the data [2].

B_paper_rr24.question: what methods were used to reduce data sparsity effects?
B_paper_rr24.answer: The paper states that data augmentation methods are used to increase the amount of training data so that the NMT systems suffer less from the low-resourced situation in Japanese–Vietnamese translation [4]. One such method is Back Translation, in which a machine translation system translates monolingual data to create synthetic parallel data, which is then mixed with the original bilingual data to train the NMT system [4]. In this work, an amount of Vietnamese monolingual data is subsampled so that the synthetic corpus has the same size as the Japanese–Vietnamese parallel corpus, doubling the data size compared to the original [3][4]. Another data augmentation method considered useful in this low-resourced setting is the mix-source method, which utilizes monolingual data of the target language in a multilingual NMT system by mixing the original source sentences with target monolingual data [3]. Specifically, a parallel corpus is generated from the monolingual corpus to model the identical translation Y-Y, and then it is mixed with the original parallel corpus, with Vietnamese sentence pairs subsampled so that the parallel data size is also doubled [3]. To let the NMT know which language a certain source sentence is in, language tags are appended to every word in both source and target sentences of the mixed corpus [3]. The paper also notes that to deal with rare-word translation problems, translation units are experimented with at different levels: subword, word and beyond [1].

A_global_rr24.question: How is the vocabulary of word-like or phoneme-like units automatically discovered?
A_global_rr24.answer: The vocabulary of word-like units is discovered through unsupervised term discovery (UTD), which creates hard clusters of repeated word-like units in raw speech [1]. In UTD, graph edges are thresholded and each connected component of the graph is a cluster of acoustic segments, producing a corresponding term (word/phrase) category, with each discovered term category consisting of a list of term occurrences [5]. For phoneme-like units, a phone-loop model is formulated where each phoneme-like unit is modeled as an HMM with a Gaussian mixture model of output densities (GMM-HMM) [2]. Under the Dirichlet process framework, the phone loop is considered an infinite mixture of GMM-HMMs, with mixture weights based on the stick-breaking construction of the Dirichlet process [2]. The infinite number of units in the mixture is truncated in practice, giving zero mixture weight to any unit beyond some large count [2]. This mixture of GMM-HMMs is treated as a single unified HMM, so segmentation of the data is performed using the standard forward-backward algorithm [2]. Training is fully unsupervised and parallelized; after a fixed number of training iterations, the Viterbi decoding algorithm is used to obtain acoustic unit tokenizations of the data [2].
